title: Re J. (A Minor) (Abduction: Custody Rights) [1990] 2 AC 562, [1990] 2 All ER 961, [1990] 2 FLR 450, sub nom C. v. S. (A Minor) (Abduction)
text:
FACTS

The child, a boy, was 2 1/3 at the date of the alleged wrongful removal. He had lived in Western Australia all of his life. The parents were not married and the father had no custody rights in respect of the boy. On 21 March 1990 the mother took the boy to England, her State of origin.

On 12 April 1990 the father was awarded sole guardianship and custody by the Family Court of Western Australia and on 26 April the same court made a declaration that the removal of the boy was wrongful.
 
On 19 April 1990 the Australian authorities made an application for the summary return of the child. On 30 April 1990 the English High Court ruled that there had neither been a wrongful removal nor a wrongful retention. This ruling was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 17 May 1990.

The father appealed.

---

RULING

Appeal dismissed and application dismissed; there had neither been a wrongful removal or retention as the child had lost his Australian habitual residence when he left that State with his mother.

---

GROUNDS

Habitual Residence - Art. 3


Habitual residence is a factual concept, to be understood according to the ordinary and natural meaning of the two words it contains. A habitual residence may be lost in a day if there is a settled intention not to return. To become habitual a period of residence must have endured for an appreciable period of time and the individual must have a settled intention to so reside.

Where a young child has only one custodian the child's habitual residence will necessarily be the same as that of the custodian. On the facts the child lost his habitual residence in Western Australia upon leaving that State.

Rights of Custody - Art. 3

Rights of Custody - Sources of Custody Rights 

At the time of the removal the mother had sole custody of the child. The subsequent attribution of custody rights to the father could not render the removal wrongful. The UK courts were not bound by the finding of the Australian court in this regard.

Procedural Matters

It may be noted that only 3 1/2 months elapsed between the return application being lodged and the second appellate court decision.
